opus-5.5.text:
I think AlphaGo is one of those rare projects where the whole history of AI kind of passes through a single system. You've got search, you've got learned value functions, you've got policy networks, you've got self-play, and they all have to work together. When you rebuild it yourself, you can't hand-wave any of those pieces. You actually have to understand why Monte Carlo tree search needs a good prior, why the value network matters, and how self-play bootstraps you out of the limits of human data.

The other thing that's compelling is that it's a very clean testbed. Go has a perfect simulator, unambiguous rewards, and a crisp notion of getting better, because you can just play the old version against the new one. In a lot of modern AI work, especially with large language models, evaluation is murky. You're never quite sure whether the model actually improved or you just moved the benchmark. With Go, the board tells you the truth.

And then there's a nostalgia and a forward-looking piece at the same time. A lot of people in the field, myself included, got pulled into deep learning partly because of that 2016 moment with Lee Sedol, move 37 and all that. But I also think the ideas in AlphaGo, using search plus learned intuition to generate better training data than you started with, are extremely relevant again now. That's essentially what people are trying to do with reasoning models and RL on top of language models. So rebuilding AlphaGo with today's hardware and tools is partly a way of asking: what did we actually learn, what was essential, and what was just engineering for 2016 compute? You find out that a lot of it you can do on a much smaller budget now, and that tells you something about where the real insights were.

r001.rationale: The candidate lists AlphaGo’s components and notes that search needs a good prior, but it does not state that AlphaGo demonstrated deep learning could handle Go despite the game’s intractability for search.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not express puzzlement about a shallow neural network amortizing very deep simulations; it discusses value and policy networks without that claim.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that got me hooked wasn't the result itself. Everybody knows AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol. What I found compelling was that it's one of the few systems in the history of AI where every single component is load-bearing, and you can actually see what each one is doing.

You have a policy network that encodes intuition, basically a prior over what a strong player would consider. You have a value network that's a learned sense of "how is this position going for me." And then you have search, which is the deliberate, System 2 part, where you spend compute to correct the mistakes of your intuition. Rebuilding it forces you to ask: how much of the strength comes from each piece? If I rip out the search, how much do I lose? If I make the value network worse, does the search compensate? Those are questions you can't really answer by reading the paper. You have to get your hands dirty.

The other thing is that it's a closed loop. The policy is trained from self-play, which is generated by the search, which is guided by the policy. That's a flywheel, and when flywheels work in machine learning they feel almost magical, but they're also incredibly finicky. Small bugs don't crash your program, they just make the agent quietly plateau at an amateur level, and you have no idea why. Debugging that teaches you more about RL than any textbook.

And then there's a broader point. I think a lot of people see large language models now and assume that scale plus data is the whole story. AlphaGo is a reminder that there's a second axis, which is spending compute at inference time to think harder. The model that plays Go without search is decent, and the same model with search is superhuman. That gap is the thing I want to understand deeply, because I suspect it matters a lot for where AI goes next, in robotics and in reasoning more generally. So rebuilding it is partly nostalgia, sure, but mostly it's trying to internalize that lesson at the level of code rather than at the level of a blog post.

r001.rationale: It says AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol and highlights deep networks combined with search, but does not identify the achievement as deep learning handling Go despite the game’s intractability for search.

r002.rationale: It describes policy and value networks guiding search, but expresses no puzzlement about how a relatively shallow network can amortize simulations deep into the game tree.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is the way it combines learning and search. You have a neural network that gives you an intuition about which moves are promising and how good a position is. Then you spend more computation searching, and you get a better answer than that initial intuition. And you can train the network on the results of that search, so the thing you worked hard to figure out becomes something you can recognize immediately next time.

That’s a really interesting feedback loop: thinking improves your intuition, and better intuition lets you think more effectively. In Go, you can study that in a setting where the rules are precise and you get a clear signal about whether you’re improving.

Rebuilding it forces you to understand how that loop actually works. It’s easy to say, “You combine a policy network, a value network, and tree search.” But how do you allocate the search? What makes the training stable? Why does each component help? Getting the whole system to work would give me a much deeper understanding than just reading the paper.

r001.rationale: It describes combining neural networks with search and learning from search results, but does not say AlphaGo showed deep learning could handle Go despite Go’s intractability for search.

r002.rationale: It discusses using more computation for search but does not express puzzlement about a relatively shallow network amortizing simulations far down Go’s game tree.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s compelling to me is that you can start with the rules of a game and, through learning and search, discover strategies that humans haven’t found in thousands of years of playing it. You’re not programming in what a good move looks like. You’re building a process that can figure that out for itself.

And rebuilding it forces you to understand how the pieces fit together. The policy guides the search, the value function tells you which positions are promising, and the search produces better targets for learning. There’s this feedback loop where a system can improve the very intuition it uses to decide what to think about.

That feels like a useful thing to understand beyond Go: how do you turn more computation into better decisions, and then distill those decisions into something that can act more efficiently?

r001.rationale: It says learning and search can discover new Go strategies, but does not identify AlphaGo as showing that deep learning could handle Go despite its intractability for search.
